Target / co-contaminant: Multiple antibiotics; the identity of each Table 1 pollutant must be verified
Adsorbent / material: Polysaccharide-based magnetic hydrogels containing cellulose, chitosan, alginate, carrageenan, starch or gums
Evidence domain: Secondary synthesis; synthesis, mechanism, reusability and primary-source discovery
Experimental design / conditions: Narrative review; no original adsorption experiment in this article
Reported result: Reviews preparation routes, adsorption mechanisms, reported performance and magnetic recovery; Table 1 compiles examples and Table 2 lists scale-up/research challenges.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p.1 (title/abstract); Sections 2–5, PDF pp.4–14; Table 1 PDF p.10; Table 2 PDF p.14; bibliography PDF pp.15–17
Caveat / follow-up: Do not use its numerical table values as primary evidence. Trace each claim to its original cited paper. Table 1 includes fluvastatin and diclofenac, which are not antibiotics, despite the broad table label.

Evidence domain: Reusability, stability, synthesis burden and scale-up
Reported result: Highlights degradation/fouling and loss of magnetic properties as reuse concerns; notes process complexity, cost-effective scale-up, environmental impacts and need for further mechanism and practical-water validation.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp.12–14; Section 4.3 and Sections 5.1–5.2; Table 2 PDF p.14
Caveat / follow-up: Use as context only. Any regeneration number or performance claim must be cited to the original study, not this review's summary.

Adsorbent / material: Homoionic smectites: montmorillonites SWy-2 and STx-1b; kaolinite KGa-1; isotherms mainly on K-SWy-2
Experimental design / conditions: Batch: 50 mL Milli-Q water; 0.01 g clay; ENR 1–24 mg/L; pH 3.5–8.5; 10 mM KCl/CsCl or 5 mM CaCl2; end-over-end rotation 35 rpm for 24 h at room temperature; triplicate. pH-edge figures use C0=18 mg/L.
Reported result: Tests pH, cation identity, ionic strength and humic-acid effects in controlled solution chemistry.
Model / metric: Batch sorption; pH edge and isotherm experiments
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p.2 (printed p.142), Sections 2.1–2.2; Fig.1; Fig.2 caption PDF p.3
Caveat / follow-up: Not an actual-wastewater trial. Supporting Information (Tables S1–S3 and Fig. S1) is referenced but was not supplied.

Value / units: K_F in mg^(1−n) L^n g^−1; n and R² dimensionless
Model / metric: Freundlich fit; K_F is not a Langmuir q_max
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p.3 (printed p.143), Table 1 and Section 3.1; Fig.1 on PDF p.2
Caveat / follow-up: Very low n (0.08–0.12) indicates strongly nonlinear fitting. Keep the source units; do not treat K_F as q_max or directly compare it with mg/g capacities.

Experimental design / conditions: pH-edge experiments at C0=18 mg/L; reported ENR pKa values 6.27 and 8.30.
Reported result: Sorption rose from pH 3.5 to a maximum around pH 5.5, then declined. The authors report >98% cationic ENR at pH 3.5–4.5; at pH 8.5, 38.6% zwitterionic and 61.2% anionic species. Sorption remained >85% from pH 6.5 to 7.5 even when the cationic fraction was below 10%.
Value / units: Sorption percentage and speciation percentages as reported
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p.3 (printed p.143), Section 3.1 and Fig.2; speciation Fig. S1 is in unavailable SI
Caveat / follow-up: The authors propose surface protonation as a possible explanation for high mid-pH sorption. Keep that as a hypothesis, not a proven mechanism.

Adsorbent / material: SWy-2, STx-1b and kaolinite; K-, Ca- and Cs-saturated SWy-2
Evidence domain: Cation selectivity, ionic strength, mineral comparison and dissolved organic matter
Experimental design / conditions: HA additions: 1 mg/L Fluka HA and 5 mg/L Suwannee River HA; ionic strength series 10, 50 and 100 mM KCl.
Reported result: Cation selectivity was K > Ca > Cs. The authors' interpretation reports cation-exchange-derived sorption decreasing from about 80% to about 50% as KCl increased from 0.01 to 0.10 M. Smectites sorbed more ENR than kaolinite; SWy-2 sorbed more than STx-1b. HA had a marginal overall effect under tested conditions.
Value / units: Order comparison; model-interpreted fraction about 80% to 50%
Model / metric: pH-edge and electrolyte series / PHREEQC interpretation
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p.3, Fig.2 and Section 3.1; PDF p.4, Figs.3–4 and Sections 3.2–3.3
Caveat / follow-up: Do not generalize the weak HA effect to all real waters: this used specified HA types and concentrations in controlled electrolyte.

Evidence domain: Cation exchange, surface complexation and interlayer adsorption
Experimental design / conditions: ATR–FTIR, XRD, and PHREEQC-supported interpretation; FTIR wash/desorption tests are a mechanistic diagnostic, not a treatment regeneration cycle.
Reported result: Authors conclude that outer-sphere cation exchange and inner-sphere surface complexation both contribute to ENR sorption. XRD supports interlayer ENR, with d001 increasing from 1.33 to 1.71 nm as ENR loading increased to 20 mg/g clay. HA did not change d001 under tested conditions.
Value / units: d001 1.33→1.71 nm; ENR loading 20 mg/g clay
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p.5, Fig.5 / Section 3.4; PDF p.6, Fig.6 / Section 3.5 and conclusion
Caveat / follow-up: Interlayer expansion supports intercalation but is not equivalent to a deployable treatment capacity. No real wastewater, column or regeneration-cycle study.

Adsorbent / material: Na-montmorillonite (Na-MONT) with Ca2+ or Mg2+ in solution
Experimental design / conditions: 20 mL of 320 μM OTC with 20 mg Na-MONT; background 0.01 M NaNO3 and 5 mM each acetate/bicarbonate buffer; pH 4, 6 or 8; pH maintained within ±0.1 for 40 h. Main Ca/Mg tests used equimolar cation and OTC.
Reported result: Controlled mechanistic batch experiments; UV–vis quantification with FTIR, solid-state NMR, experimental XRD and simulated XRD for mechanism testing.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p.3 (printed p.155), Section 2.1; Fig.1 caption and conditions PDF p.2 (printed p.154)
Caveat / follow-up: Model-clay experiment, not real wastewater. Conditions are limited to specified pH values, cation ratios and high controlled feed concentration.

Adsorbent / material: Na-montmorillonite with and without Ca2+ or Mg2+
Experimental design / conditions: OTC adsorption compared at pH 4, 6 and 8 with a 1:1 metal:OTC ratio.
Reported result: Adsorption increased by up to about 80% at pH 6 and 120% at pH 8 in the presence of Ca or Mg; at pH 4 adsorption was similar with and without those cations. The authors report up to 261 mmol OTC/kg clay at pH 4 and 54 mmol OTC/kg clay at pH 8 without the metal-promoted effect.
Value / units: Relative increase under specified conditions; reported sorbed amounts in mmol OTC/kg clay
Model / metric: Observed clay-associated amount; not removal percent or fitted q_max
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p.2, Fig.1B; PDF p.3 (printed p.155), Section 2.1; PDF pp.3–4, Section 3.1
Caveat / follow-up: 80% and 120% are relative increases under specified pH and equimolar conditions—not removal percentages and not a general effect for all metal concentrations.

Evidence domain: Mechanistic interpretation: cation-mediated adsorption and interlayer trapping
Experimental design / conditions: FTIR, 1H–13C CPMAS NMR, experimental XRD and simulated XRD; compares Mg:OTC solution ratios 1:1 and 1:4.
Reported result: Spectroscopy did not strongly support an inner-sphere ternary metal–OTC–clay complex as the necessary mechanism; the dimethylamino group mediated adsorption with and without divalent cations. At pH 8, 1:1 Mg:OTC shifted d001 from about 1.28 to 1.72 nm. Diluting Mg:OTC from 1:1 to 1:4 reduced d001 from about 1.70 to 1.28 nm and reduced the modeled OTC-containing MONT layers from 60% to 20%.
Value / units: d001 in nm; modeled fraction of OTC-containing layers in % under stated simulated conditions
Model / metric: FTIR/NMR plus experimental and simulated XRD
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp.4–6 (printed pp.156–158), Figs.2–3 and Sections 3.2–3.5
Caveat / follow-up: Authors argue interlayer trapping and clay aggregation/interstratification better explain the promoted adsorption; weaker outer-sphere bridging is not excluded. No real-water, column or regeneration study.
